Nowhere on the site, the box, or the manual mentions that the app requires precise location in order to operate. Just like Bluetooth that is required. Why is Bluetooth mentioned as required, but not GPS?
Why does a hydrometer require your location to operate? On the iPhone if you share your location, but turn off 'Precise Location', it won't work. It must be precise location. Why?! If the answer is Altitude, why is that not explain. Why not provide a way to enter altitude. Why if I'm brewing in a basement where GPS doe snort work anyway?

Very sneaky and non-transparent. Avoid devices and apps that won't work without knowing your exact location!

Have a few different FDM printers of my own and got this for my son to learn on. Good quality so far and the filament dryer is huge plus so I don’t have to buy a separate one and it’s powered by the printer so no extra power cords needed. Downside is that I can only really use it for this printer. I would love to be able to use it for my other printers as well. Build volume is really nice so we can print some larger pieces and not worry about space.

Set up was quick and very easy! I took about an hour of extra time making sure everything was perfectly squared, levelled, and tightened the way that I wanted it to be but that’s me being picky. I really feel like that went along way in getting good prints right off the hop!

I do really like the magnetic build surface. It stick to the prints really nicely and makes it really easy to get prints off the bed without using a tool. Bed levelling seems pretty good right off the bat but I would suggest doing a good levelling yourself to get a good and lasting level. I ended up having to level it manually with paper first. The build volume is a huge benefit to us for being able to print off larger parts and things like helmets and costume parts for my son.

Touch screen is very easy to use and navigate. Much better than the knob style screen!

Only things I really don’t like are things that are due to my own preferences and

Son is happy with it so far and I’m impressed with the quality of prints we get right away. Seems like a good printer for beginners like us.

To start; I’m not new to 3D printing at all. I recieved the CR Touch and as others have said the instructions that are included are garbage. The instructions on where to download the firmware are no longer accurate but Google and YouTube were helpful in locating it. I installed the CR Touch, installed the correct firmware and set the Z Offset (distance between nozzle and probe).  Then used the auto bed leveling and went to do my first print. That’s when the issues started. My bed had been manually leveled and was printing fine. After using the automatic bed leveling my prints started to fail in the first few layers. 3/4 of the print would adhere and 1/4 of it would try to print in the air, as though the printer was trying to accommodate for a thoroughly unlevel bed. So I used the CR Touch to level the bed again and recorded the Z values that it reported at each of the 9 points, made adjustments and ran the bed leveling again. I spent about 2 hours chasing a level bed using this method, making small changes and then re-running the auto bed leveling. Finally I ran the auto bed leveling 3 times in a row by making no changes at all and recieved Z values that were as much as 1.4mm off from the same exact spot on previous runs with no changes. Based on this I concluded that this probe has no idea where it is or where my bed is and that’s why it’s trying to print in midair for part of my print, because as I stated my Z offset is correct.

Pros:
*No battery
*Simple, robust design (vernier)
*mm scale is easy to read

Cons:
*Inches scale is at least 0.006 inches short
*Depth post is about 0.4 mm short (see photo)
*mm scale will not zero (see photo)
*Hard to read inches scale, even with reading glasses
*No fine adjustment wheel (anticipated at this price)

See my recommendations at the end for something better.

I was really excited about this caliper because I wanted a simple measuring tool with no batteries and no delicate/fragile dial. I knew the inches scale was decimal rather than fractional, which apparently many buyers don't understand. The build quality is not exceptional, but that is expected given the price. My first issue was trying to read the inches scale. I'm in my mid 40s, and the tick marks on the main body scale are so small and close together that I had to use a magnifying glass to see where the marks on the sliding scale lined up in the vernier method. Fortunately, I had no problem reading the mm scale unaided.

I found the next problem while testing accuracy with a dial caliper and a digital caliper. I found this caliper to be 0.006 inches short, as verified by both other calipers. Since both the hundredths and thousandths places must be obtained by some effort for inches (due to the vernier method), including some addition if the segment is greater than 0.25, this makes it unlikely I would ever measure anything to any greater degree of accuracy than to a tenth of an inch (0.1 in). In spite of that, I thought I would keep the caliper, mainly for use in measuring millimeters, which it seems to do fairly accurately. The photo might show why mm is more accurate, since the mm scale will not zero all the way. Perhaps a good way to introduce error at the farther end of the scale…

Then I noticed the depth gauge. While fully recessed, it is clear that the depth measurement post is not flush with the end of the scale (as seen in the photo). I compared measurements with the digital caliper, and sure enough, the depth gauge would give readings that were about 0.7 mm too long (because the depth post is too short). In the end, I find these problems too great to make it worth keeping, and I would recommend you avoid this product. No doubt some units produced will be better than others, but if I wanted decent accuracy I would not take another chance with a replacement of this same item--too many problems in one sample.

At worst, it can be considered dishonest to market a measuring tool which purports to give measurements accurate to 0.001, when that measurement will not be right.

Although I have not yet found a very accurate AND inexpensive vernier caliper, I would recommend the following if you want to avoid batteries. They are very easy to read and do not require the extra time and steps taken to obtain measurements by the vernier method:

For fractional inches: Shop Fox D3208 Fractional Dial Caliper

For decimal inches and mm: Anytime Tools Dial Caliper 6" / 150mm DUAL Reading Scale METRIC SAE Standard INCH MM

They are both at least twice the cost, but still much less expensive than the premium brands, and I find them to be very accurate and reliable. And no batteries required.

As we all can read, PETG is hygroscopic meaning it absorbs water out of thin air. So you must dehydrate it somehow to prepare it for use. I use a food dehydrator and monitor it's progress with an electronic meter that checks temperature and humidity. At the most the temperature got up to 126 degrees F, but mostly averaged 118'F. This should not be a high enough temperature to negatively affect the filament (149'f is recommended, but I can't even get it up that high).

So after a number of hours dehydrating, I put it to use trying to print. The first 1/4 spool went OK, with a few issues, but then all of a sudden I found the whole spool is now bonded to itself, and any attempt to break it free would provide at the most 3' of filament before it broke off. Eventually, I could not even get more than 1/8" off of it before it broke -- if I could even pry that much off.

That being said, I cannot recommend this filament.
I will update this if Sunlu wishes to contact me to send me another spool of PETG to try.

Cons:
-IT WON'T SELF EMPTY PET HAIR. This is a total deal breaker and I feel the result of a bone head design flaw.

I thought since the 2014 review they'd have this lined out, but it is as all reviews have stated - it is not unipolar. It is latching and requires flipping the magnet to get it to switch back off.

Being my first time using these, I thought they would behave like a reed switch - either passing full voltage or not. I found I needed to use a 10K pull-up on the output lead when the magnet was away. This pulls it up to whatever voltage you need to represent digital high voltage. When the magnet is near, it goes straight to ground on the output pin so it can be readily detectable. However, most microcontrollers will have an internal resistor you can set to pull it up without the need of an external resistor.

I used a rare earth magnet and could switch it almost an inch away which was good for my application.

Having owned robotic vacuums almost since the beginning (I bought my first Roomba in 2004), I can say I have never been so excited and then so disappointed as with the Ecovacs Ozmo ECOVACS Deebot T8 AIVI and the attachment for better scrubbing.

This is a 1000 dollars investment that started failing almost from the beginning, showing a level of unreliability I have never witnessed in any other robotic brand, including Roomba, Neato, Samsung and roborock. I own all these brands, and with the exception of replacing the lithium-ion battery, most of these units have been running strong for more than a decade, some close to 15 years.

The ECOVACS Deebot works really well when it works. It is quiet and suction is good. Its navigational system is mediocre (it often will hit cables and get stuck with our kids' toys, but it does the job). It does not negotiate one of our thresholds well enough, so often gets stuck there and the app is half cooked, with poor explanations and often with bad English.

The problem is that it has been a terribly unreliable robot. Its lidar often gets stuck, and the recommended solution is to tap hard. This used to do the trick until it didn't. Less than a year and a half after I purchased it, I had to send it back for repairs, and the lidar stopped working. We do use the vacuum once a day, but I am super careful with it. After contacting ecovacs, they first declined to fix it as it was out of warranty, even though a 1000 dollars piece of equipment failing that early is just wrong. They finally agreed to take and perform the repairs, but less than two months later (3, but one it was not used as we were out of town) the system failed again. This time it is the anti-drop sensors.

It turns out you can look on a search engine how these sensors often become rusty due to a faulty design that brings the moisture of the mopping to them. Even if you remove the mopping tray after each use (which I do) water may remain on the lines, and many people complain about this damage. In the car world, all of these vacuums would be recalled due to a manufacturing defect, but here you're left with an expensive piece of robotic debris. The worst part is that they just had my vacuum with them a few months ago, so they could have checked the antidrop sensors for this known defect.

All in all, unless you're ok changing vacuums frequently, deebots are exciting products with a lot of high tech, but also a terrible execution in the way that technology is integrated. The worst part is that the company, being aware of these kinks, will not stand behind its products. Now that more established brands actually have better navigation algorithms, and integrate their sensors much better, I have stopped recommending the Deebot to friends. If you are going to use the mopping function, this brand is not for you as the anti-drop sensors may rust even when used according to the manufacturer's instructions.

These nozzles are cut wrong for most sizes. The diameter B of the tip must be 2.5 times the diameter A of hole, see the E3D engineering drawing, rev v8.1. This is true of all nozzle specs from 0.25mm to 1mm. (The document can be found at E3D-online under dozuki as a PDF (Guides -> Nozzles).) But the 0.2 and 0.3 mm nozzles Seloky sold me both have B=1.0mm, whereas they should be 0.5mm and 0.75mm. (There's no official 0.2mm spec though.) I tested the 0.2mm nozzle: it deforms sharp corners as the tip grabs on to twice the width (1mm instead of 0.5mm) of already laid down plastic. In other words, it doesn't work, or rather, it works as a 0.4 mm nozzle. For the wider extrusion diameters, the nozzle is too narrow, B is less than is should be, and that'll lead to groves visible on top surfaces.

The 0.4mm nozzle appears correct. DON'T BUY unless you can use the 0.4mm nozzles.

About 20% of the plugs in the package are poorly made - very roughly finished. If you do purchase this product, buy considerable extra than what you actually need. The quality is very poor and will take much longer to install than well-made plugs.

My solution was to drill a sequence of 1/2" holes in a scrap piece of oak plywood. Then drill a 1/8" hole through the bottom of each Forstner hole. Install the oak plugs into the holes and apply reasonable pressure to seat them as you would in your project. Take that to the belt sander and sand off the part of the plugs that protrude above the plywood. Then use a little length of metal wire to poke through the 1/8" holes drilled through the plywood (from the back) to release the plugs. Cheap materials are not cheap, when you consider the extra work that goes into using them.

I bought these awhile back. If you use them as instructed, they are effective. HOWEVER, if you don't drill these to the EXACT correct depth, then snap off the head, you will have a VERY SHARP piece of metal shooting out of your carpet just waiting to BLOODY an foot unlucky enough to find it. And GOOD LUCK getting the headless screw out of the floor. I had to use vice-grips and a LOT of elbow grease to turn them back out. So I had to roll back my carpet anyway.

Also, it's extremely easy to miss, or barely hit, the floor joist you're looking for, which will cause you a LOT of time, frustration, and MANY of these little Squeek No More screws. Plus, in some homes (like MINE) the joists will change direction or be spaced incorrectly. This means a LOT, and I mean, a LOT of searching and drilling unnecessary holes throughout your carpet.

In short, please understand that I really admire this inventor's creativity. I LOVE anything gadget, tool, or invention that will make my house repairs easier, but with this one, do the smart thing - ROLL YOUR CARPET BACK, GET YOURSELF SOME SQUARE-HEAD DECK SCREWS (1 1/2" should do) from Home Depot, USE AS MANY SCREWS AS YOU WANT. AND WHEN THE SQUEAKS ARE GONE, ROLL THE CARPET BACK IN PLACE. Unless your carpet was just installed, it will not need to be re-stretched. You simply roll it from one side of the room to the other (along with the carpet pad), screw the squeaks, then unroll it back, tap the edges with your foot (wear a boot or strong-soled shoe) or a rubber mallet, and you're ready to have beer.

I live in Chicago and got concerned about lead in my soil, so I ordered this kit. I tested 4 areas of my property and all of them came back over 400 PPM. I panicked. I contemplated selling the house because if I can't garden on my property, what is the point? Anyway, I looked at other reviews of people saying they got false positives with this kit. I searched for a lab to do a REAL soil test and my local Farm Bureau office hooked me up with a full-fledged soil test for $58. Lab results came back for lead at 61.4 PPM; my soil is completely safe to garden in.
This product does have a disclaimer that other heavy metals or whatever may give you a false positive.... but if that's the case, then what are we doing here? Stop it. Further, apparently in order to perform a proper lead analysis, it takes a lot longer than 5 minutes. This kit is a scam- don't buy it! Save yourself some time, money and anxiety by just getting a proper lab test done on your soil.

I tried to look at my hand first, I could only get a clear picture when I press the tip against my palm. This made ear examination impossible ----- you will never get a clear picture of the tympanic membrane(TM) unless you physically touch the TM with your tip (but who does that?!!!). I tried all the tips provided in the kit, but none of them could provide a clear picture of the TM. The best picture I got was a blurry blurry blurry "cone of light" (almost could not tell). Also, the original tip was full of dust inside. The dust will reflect the LED light and you will see a "snowy dust" before you see anything in the ear.

3. OPTHALMOSCOPE: The LED light is not bright enough. I could barely see the red/orange hue when first shining the light into the eye (possibly due to insufficient lighting and cold LED light color). Also, the magnifying lens on the ophthalmoscope is not clear neither, there is NO WAY to do a fundoscopic exam because I could not see any details of the retina.

4. LIGHTING: horrible. A traditional scope's light is supposed to be bright, warm/orange color. This thing is a somber, cold hue, from one tiny LED light bulb.

5. BATTERY: uses 2 C-cell batteries. C-cell batteries are not convenient. Plus, if you decide to implement C-CELL X2 which provides more mAh, why do you still make the light so dark??????

These are nearly impossible to drive all the way into concrete. I bought a box and used them to secure 2x4s and they seemed difficult, but not too terrible. The impact driver would frequently jump out of the screw. Months later, I then tried to secure an elfa top bracket into concrete, which means driving it 1.5" deeper than before. EVERY single screw either stopped driving or the impact driver jumped out.

I am doing everything I did with tapcon. I drill with a 3/16" SDS bit an inch deeper than the screw then vacuum out the hole. I then drive the screw with a square bit using a newer high end DeWalt impact driver set on the 2nd speed. Tapcons weren't easy, but weren't THAT much worse than wood screws. These, I have to lean into the driver an unsafe degree. I tried using new screw bits and the fancy impact bits, just lots of frustration and marks on the wall from when the impact driver jumped out of the screw.

I tried varying the speed, but with confast, the impact driver is either going too slow to move or the driver jumps out of the screw head and damages everything.

I gave up in frustration and bought a box of tapcons and was able to finish the job with no drama, maybe 1 screw jump total out of 10 instead of 3x per screw. I ruined like 6 screw bits and probably 15 screws messing around with CONFAST...not the biggest of deals, but nothing I've ever seen before.

So if you're buying CONFAST, only drive small screws. Also, buy a ton more than you actually need and only use them on things you want to mount the wall that you're not worried about damaging when they seize up in your wall and your impact driver jumps out.

I bought this probe to replace the previous probe which did the exact same thing.

Here's what it does, works fine for about six months, temperature set to turn the aquarium heater on at 72 degrees and off at 73 degrees. Running a 150 watt heater. After about six months, suddenly the low temperature alarm is going off, emergency, fish cold, help!

Glance at the submerged thermometer, it's reading 78 degrees, way too hot!

UPDATE 6/24/2018 These are definitely not 100% copper. Even after annealing I get seepage on perfectly clean banjos in a clutch system. They just aren't soft enough to seal. The 40 year-old, new-old-stock copper washers I used with this system were perfect after cleaning all the verdigris and annealing but this garbage won't seal. It's not a huge leak or anything just a tiny bit of seepage after 10 or 15 applications of the clutch - Still unacceptable.

UPDATE 6/18/2018 Unfortunately although these seemed good at first I've found some issues with the 'copper' that is used to make them. They don't 'give' nearly as well as better quality copper washers. I believe they are either an alloy of copper or they are work hardened from the manufacturing process. I've had some that wouldn't seal in a zero-pressure situation - banjo fitting on a brake reservoir line. I've had others that worked fine. At this point I won't use them unless I anneal them first which is annoying. Bottom line, they're okay in an emergency if you have nothing else.

ORIGINAL REVIEW - I am pleasantly surprised by the quality of the washers in this kit. Normally I don't expect much from anything made in china but these copper washers are an exception. If you work on ancient British cars you need alot of copper washers in non-metric sizes. The washers in this little set are actually quite thick, in fact when I compared the original 1/2" oil gallery plug copper washers from a Jag XK engine to these they are the same thickness as the ones I'm replacing (a little smaller in diameter though) - like I said, surprising.... and at .18 cents a washer the price is certainly better than buying them piece by piece from a specialty supplier.

I purchased this device thinking that it would detect the various objects inside the wall. It does this by packaging multiple sensors in the device, a capacitive studfinder, metal detector, and a 10Ghz doppler motion detector. The software then displays the detected object on the screen depending on the sensor input. Out of curiosity on how things work I opened up the unit. I can only think that I was sent an early prototype, I've never seen so much glop and silcone rubber covering connectors and other objects in the unit. There was a kludge board with 6 blue wires added to the main board.

As a wood studfinder it is only fair, there are better dedicated studfinders available that are much more sensitive.

For metal detection, it often displayed a live copper wire as a copper pipe. Othertimes it would sometimes display the incorrect object type, ie wood stud instead of plastic or metal.

In using the unit I was getting errors to hold the device against the wall, there was a slight texture to the sheetrock paint, and perhaps that confused it.

Using the device you have to move it a controlled speed, the display just indicates too fast or too slow.

For the list price of this unit you could purchase: a studfinder, and metal detector with AC detection for much less money. The only thing the Dewalt would do for you is to detect the plastic pipe if it is within range, and it has a very nice color display.

I have a Roborock s5 which means I pretty much never have to vacuum or mop. I just need a vacuum to get into cracks/crevices, vacuum my couch of pet hair, and to do a more thorough cleaning of the carpet every couple of months. This vacuum is lightweight and easily carried. The hose attaches easily and can change attachments no problem. No installation needed just plug hose in and good to go. The issues are:
1) Cord length. I have a small single bedroom apartment and I figured it would be no problem to just unplug once or twice to move it to another outlet. Wrong. 2) Primary attachment head is awful. The suction is strong which is great but the vacuum head does not have wheels so it just suctions onto the floor and does not want to move. You have to stay bent over and use extra strength to push it along the floor. And even then it is difficult. But the worst were my throw rugs. It would not let me move the hose along the rug because it would just suck it up and bunch it up. Not even standing on a couple corners to hold it down would work.
3) Poor pickup. Although the suction was strong, afted I vacuumed my throw rug (which was a crazy difficult task for the reason above) I shook it out after I had vacuumed it over both directions several times and dust and debris still flew off the rug. So I'm not impressed with how well it cleans either.
4) It was a lot better on hard wood floors but still a terrible vacuum. And if you have throw rugs on your hardwood then I absolutely do not recommend this vacuum.

Should have listened to the negative reviews... I have fiddled with my Englander pellet stove enough times now that replacing an auger motor should take 15 minutes. This took 3 hours. First of all, after getting the motor set in place, it turned until it wedged itself between the top and bottom motor shelves (only took 5 seconds for that to happen). So I figured it's backward, so I'll follow the directions to flip it. Despite the directions mislabeling parts I was able to figure out this simple chore. Put the motor back in place. Same deal. It turned in the SAME direction and got wedged. So I thought maybe I was dumb and didn't actually flip the magnet directed to flip. So I did it again. This time it would not turn at all, the pellet stove power cut out suddenly, and I'm pretty sure the fuser is blown. I was really hoping to have this stove running for freezing temps over the weekend (in the middle of April).

I got a fuse, fired it up, and same thing. It would turn for a bit and then get stuck. In troubleshooting I had to turn the bottom auger manually to get the motor piston back in place, but it wouldn't turn. I realized that it dropped pellets to the lower part, that had been spinning in reverse, and created a nightmare of a problem that could have been avoided if this product came with some directions or warnings. Even a simple label on the motor forward and backward would have helped. I don't know what direction the motor spins in, but it was opposite of my Englander and caused a 5.5 hour project. Things are working now, but I stand by my score.

I love my Kamado Joe Classic III, but I hate babysitting dome temperatures during long smokes. Without spending too much time evaluating the alternatives, I purchased this item based on the brand name alone, thinking that it would be designed as well as the rest of the Kamado Joe accessory line up.

Well, that's the last time I make that mistake.

Unit #1 performed well for about 10 cooks. I loved the data accumulated in the app from previous cooks, as it helps me to plan how long future cooks may take. But then with no change to the location of my grill or to my WiFi setup, the iKamand started dropping the WiFi connection. As stated in the instructions, occasional disconnections from WiFi are nothing to worry about, but the disconnections I experienced were difficult or impossible to recover from.

In practice, this means that when you're 7 hours into smoking a brisket and not only does the unit lose connection to WiFi but also doesn't notify you that the connection is severed, you'll be scrambling to remove the unit and replace it with a standard plate that you can manually regulate the dome temperature. That is, if you notice it has lost its connection at all.

With two cooks nearly ruined, I returned this unit for a replacement.

Unit #2 did not survive even one cook before permanently losing its WiFi connection. I tried multiple 2.4 GHz networks as well as using my iPhone as a hotspot, which should work according to the instructions. There was no way to get this unit to connect to the Internet and stay connected.

If you're considering buying this product, you may be thinking, "This may work fine for me; I may not have the WiFi issues that he's having." That is true. If this didn't have WiFi connectivity issues, I'd probably give it 3 stars. When it works, it works, but I would definitely improve the app in terms of alerts (this should be loud, repeating, and un-ignorable, but I can very easily miss "temp reached" notifications with one overly-polite notification). However, there is a particular problem with lack of WiFi connectivity that kills the usability of this device that you should strongly consider in any case:

THIS UNIT MUST BE CONTROLLED VIA APP OVER WIFI. IT CANNOT BE SET OR ADJUSTED OTHERWISE.

It follows that with any transient connection problem with your phone, the app, or WiFi, the iKamand is only useful as a paperweight.

If you've read this far and you've never bought a similar device, here are some questions to ask yourself before choosing a temperature controller:
1. Does the device need to be programmable sans an app or a network?
2. Are audible/loud alerts desired?
3. Does the device need to be controllable by Bluetooth (in case WiFi is unavailable)?
4. Should the device have a physical display to indicate its current state?
5. Should the temperature monitoring of this device be usable even without the grill?

If you answered yes to any of these questions, this device will leave you disappointed and possibly frustrated. If you answered yes to all of these questions, you'll be much better served by a ThermoWorks Sense + Billows combo or maybe the Flame Boss, the latter of which is available on Amazon.

For background, I'm a professional machinist, not a hobbyist.  I have a job for a customer making special sockets and need to broach 1/2" drive holes.  Since I don't need it often, I decided to take a chance on a cheaper tool for this one job.  Big mistake.  To start with, the pilot is too large in diameter to fit in a 1/2" hole.  Pretty hard to make a 1/2" square hole if you have to start with a round hole much larger than that.  Since I'm time constrained on this job, I decided to grind the pilot to the correct size and try the broach.  The first cutting surface on the broach is too aggressive and I had to stop on the first attempt as I was about to break the broach in the press trying to get it to cut. If all you need is a 1/2"ish size hole in an non-precision application, and are cutting soft materials, then maybe this will work for you.  The better choice would  be to by a better tool.

Purchased the RE300 from T.E.Dep. and was shipped a unit with a dry probe. Unit provided inconsistent and unreliable readings. T.E.Dep. refused to take it back (was at day 45 from purchase) so they brushed me off with the "no returns period" statement and pointed me to the manufacture to get it replaced.

Contacted manufacturer and was shipped a replacement probe which turned out to be even more unreliable than the one it was replacing. The replacement unit gives readings all over the place when sampling the same solution over and over. If the probe is left in the sample, it will give a reading of 0mv after about 3 minutes.

Contacted manufacturer again (Frank) and was given a "that's interesting" response when I explained the results I was getting. He forwarded me to Tech Support where I ended up in voice mail. I called right back and the lady who answered the phone made arrangements to send me another replacement.

If the 2nd replacement works, I'll adjust my rating accordingly.

Just received the replacement of the replacement and it too is absolutely unreliable. Soak in distilled water (or tap) for 10 minutes, turn on, swish into solution to be tested, wait 1 to 3 minutes for stable reading. Reading never stabilizes and removing the probe, turning it off and back on again and into the solution gives yet a different reading than the one just before it and it is off by over 50 Mv.

The unit is made in china and I'm betting that the age of the probe having traveled that far may have a lot to do with why it doesn't work. It may be simply too old.

I'm going after a refund now. I'm sick of wasting my time. When I shell out 100 bucks for a probe, I expect it to work.

I've been battling with thermal issues with this thing since the moment it arrived. I've done everything from polishing the interface between my heatsink and hotend and applying thermal paste to the threads to threading it so deeply into the heatsink block that I had to customize my fan ducts for the nozzle to clear them, and I'm still having issues with jamming due to the filament melting prematurely in the tube. This has led to the odd situation in which I can print ABS just fine, but not PLA due to its lower melting point.

The thermal insulation between the heat block and the rest of the hotend needs to be vastly improved, and the tube just needs to be made longer to increase the amount of thread that can be sunk into both the heatsink and heater block. These issues coupled with the sharp taper from 2.0 to 1.75 mm lead to a perfect storm for jamming.

but then, they failed. installed these on a shop creeper type stool. worked well for about 6 months and then started to notice ball bearings on the garage floor. after close examination of the caster, I found the reason, the top cover for the bearings that looks like a large washer, only appears to be pressed on the bolt and there is about an eighth of an inch gap between the washer and what looks like a nut just above it, but is really part of the bolt, it does not move. that top bearing cover breaks loose and is then forced up to the bottom of that 'nut'. when that happens the gap where the bearings reside is now just big enough for the bearings to escape, and they do.
every caster I installed failed this way. it is a manufacturing defect. that bearing top cover needs to be welded in place, not just pressed on, or something needs to be placed between it and that 'nut' (which isn't a nut).
So fair warning on these, they start out nice, but will fail shortly there after.

I bought this shop vac for its lighter body. (I have a much larger one that is harder to maneuver around the house.) After my recent shoulder injury, I thought this lighter vacuum would be of help, but oh how my shoulder aches right now! The good part is this vacuum does suck almost as well as the larger shop vac and the assembly was easier; although, the instructions poorly explained how to affix the vacuum on the wall hanger. I am glad now that I didn't mess with that, since I am considering returning this vacuum for a refund.

The problems: First, the plug is a three-prong, grounded plug that can only be used with an adapter or a three-prong extension cord, unless you have three-prong outlets. My house has old wiring and adapters tend to loosen from the outlets and fall out during use. My larger shop vac may have a much shorter cord, but it works with a two-prong extension cord, so there is no issue with it--something to consider if you have two-prong outlets. Second, the vacuum is louder than my larger shop vac. It may be quieter than a normal vacuum, but I expected it to also be quieter than my larger shop vac. Third, the vacuum continuously fell over due to its light weight. It was very annoying having to stop and prop it back up all the time. Fourth, the main floor attachment, which allows you to go from hard floor to carpet, is garbage. At the top of it are two switches and they (on their own) kept switching between carpet and hard floor settings just by pulling the attachment across the floor. That part was completely useless and with its swivel action, it was impossible to keep it flat on the floor. If you like vacuuming the air and not your floor, you will love it. (Maybe duct tape would work to keep it still, but why waste the effort)? Fortunately, I had an excellent floor attachment on my larger shop vac, so I just hooked it onto the end of this vacuum instead. Fifth, since the suction was not quite as good, I had to make several passes over debris to make it pick up. It took me over an hour just to vacuum the kitchen alone, whereas my larger vacuum takes me 15 minutes or less. The vacuuming of my carpeted living room was also less than impressive.

Basically, my advice to anyone thinking of buying this product would be to save yourself the aggravation and either order a larger shop vac (mine is a 6-gallon,) or buy a normal vacuum. Let me reiterate that the vacuum kept tipping over the whole time. This doesn't work for me, so I will probably return this item.

The metal that crimps on the wire is much thicker. Thicker metal in every part of the terminal, actually. The Illinois ones are also much heavier. Because they're inexpensive and I know exactly how to fix them when they break. And they do break.  I WOULD NEVER RECOMMEND THESE TO SOMEONE WHO IS NOT UP TO EXPERIMENTING, TINKERING, AND REPAIRING.  Quality control is atrocious.  Customer support from the manufacturer (not necessarily the sellers) is horrendous.  The assembly instructions give the impression that they were made to confuse you on purpose.  It's so bad that it's almost funny! If you want a printer that is reliable and just prints with no worries, then you will need to spend about 4 times more than the price of an Ender 3 V2.  Even if you get lucky and your Ender 3 V2 works on the first try, you will likely have problems in the near future.  And when that time comes, I hope you have plenty of time to learn how to fix the problem.  And the next problem. And the next one too.  This is my honest review.  Best of luck to you.

So far I've gotten 3 rolls of this stuff. The first was the Easy White, and it came so tangled that I couldn't leave a print. No big deal, I thought, quick return, it happens to even the best filament brands from time to time. While I waited for my white to be replaced, I tried out the Easy Rock. Did a couple of small prints, and it was pretty decent! Until...I started getting clogs and feed failures. This filament is so cheap that it clogged both my nozzle AND my extruder. The extruder clog was so bad that I ended up just replacing the entire part! Maybe it was a temp setting, I thought, I know that particle filled PLA sometimes need a temp boost and a hardened nozzle. So after swapping out the extruder, I slapped in a hardened tungsten nozzle from Creality, I even upped the size to a 0.5mm in case the clearance was an issue for the filament. I didn't finish a single print after that using the Easy Rock. Same problem, same timing; first layer adhesion was fine, then a cluster... So I gave up on the rock and swapped out the Easy white when I got my replacement. I couldn't even get a first layer before the same clogs I was getting with the rock.

This vacuum could be amazing but a couple kinks need to be worked out. I’ve been waiting for this bot ever since I saw it at CES. We’ve had several iRobot Roomba models and a Deebot as well. This robot is much better designed than anything that iRobot makes. Our Vacuums go out every day. One upstairs and one downstairs. The Roomba slams into everything that isn’t a wall. It damages furniture legs and marks up everything. The Sweeva is gentle and doesn’t slam into everything thanks to it’s built in lidar and does an amazing job mapping the room. That being said, we’ve had some issues with it. It seems to be randomly dropping its connection to wifi. Although that seems like a minor detail, it’s a huge issue because when you try to reconnect it, the learned map is lost. That means you have to send it out for about two full cleanings before it relearns the area and let’s you rename all the rooms. Big pain for something that should be hands off. I’m hoping that I can get this resolved with TCL and make this the best robot vacuum out there but so far they haven’t responded to my “in app” complaints. Time will tell…

Update 8/10/22:
No more issues with the wifi so I’m hoping this is resolved.

Update 12/15/22:
Do not buy this vacuum. The original Sweeva I received was great aside from the initial wifi hiccup until the rubber flap on the bottom brush guard wore down and started to rub on the hardwood floors. It made an awfully loud rubbing sound. TCL was very helpful in troubleshooting and determined it was best to replace the whole vacuum. They shipped a new one to me very quickly. The problem is, right out of the box, new one will not vacuum a low profile rug without getting stuck. It seriously cannot complete a cycle without getting stuck numerous times. It constantly thinks the main roller brushes are obstructed even though they are not. TCL was helpful and sent another new vacuum. This third vacuum does the exact same thing. It works great on hard surface floors but I cannot believe it would work at all on a high pile carpet or rugs. It is essentially unusable for us because we have to create a “no go” zone for every rug in the house. It totally defeats the purpose of having a robot vacuum.

Does this jack lift? Yes. Most of the lift stroke however is in the top of the handle, so if it's under a truck and you have to do low bottom end strokes it won't lift. It also has a lowering valve that is either on or off. Period. There is no such thing as a controlled slow descent with this jack. Makes it dangerous to use IMO. You turn the handle slowly maybe a 1/4 turn if that then you feel resistance so you ease it past that and then the valve is open and the jack and load come down full speed. I went and bought a 4K jack at harbor freight that is larger, wider, heavier duty, more stable, and importantly has a nice slow valve so you can control your lowering speeds and lifts loads at any angle of the handle for 30$ cheaper than this unit. I would not recommend this jack!

Update to review 7/15/2014:
Ok - the XV-21 finally quit forever. I did replace the battery packs at about one year. New packs gave it more life. However, after another 6 months it started exhibiting a new issue. Sometimes it would get stuck somewhere while cleaning, and if I wasn't at home, the batteries would discharge to a point where the XV-21 became unresponsive. The indicator light would glow half bright green, and the unit would not show anything on the display. Putting it up against the charger did nothing. I had to disconnect the batteries and reconnect them to "reboot" the unit and it would come back to life again (wanting a recharge). This happened a few times, and now the "rebooting" process does not work either. The XV-21 is essentially dead. I contacted Neato and after a thinking about it a few days, they indicated they would replace the unit if I paid the shipping charge. That was a month ago, and no new unit has shown up. Customer service is now as unresponsive as my XV-21. So, basically, if you can afford to replace your vacuum once a year or so, the Neato XV-21 works well - but its an expensive way to clean your floors.

Initial review:
There have been a number of reviews that say the XV21 battery does not last long enough or hold enough charge. I have found the XV21 can run for about an hour and a half on one charge. While this may not seem like a lot - let me explain the advantages of the XV21 over a "dumb" robot. The XV21 seems to "plan" the cleaning of rooms quite well. In other words, it doesn't waste battery life running around randomly. It is amazing to watch it navigate even the most complex room layout, loaded with tons of chairs, tables, ottomans, whatever. When I purchased it, I saw on-line how it vacuumed a nice, empty, rectangular room and was concerned that none of our rooms were that simple. I am impressed how the vacuum navigates around the most complex furniture layouts, and still seems to waste little precious battery running over previously vacuumed areas.

The other things to consider with battery life is that the XV21 really contains quite a powerful vacuum compared with the Roomba 500 we had before. This vacuum does tend to make it noisier than the Roomba - but we run it while we are at work, so the extra noise is not an issue. The XV21 also does a good job at returning to it's charging base for charging, and then returns to the spot it left off from to go recharge. Its fascinating to watch it think, then plan the shortest route back to the charger. It shuts off the vacuum while returning to the charger as well.

Issues:
The XV21 does have problems with surfaces that sit up a bit above the normal floor - for example, lamp bases. The XV21 can "raise" itself up to go over some changes in floor height (like rugs etc) but sometimes when it can't make it up, it will keep trying from different directions. It does eventually seem to give up and move on, but those multiple attempts do waste battery time. Also, the XV21 does pick up a lot of dirt and carpet fluff, which I guess is good, so make sure you keep on top of emptying the bin and checking the brush roller for fouling. The charging base does need to be in a location relatively free of obstructions too.

I am a pediatrician and know a few things about ear infections. I know that moms really like to be able to diagnose their own children's ear infections-- who can blame them?!-- and so cheap otoscopes like this one are very appealing and sell very well. However, as a pediatrician I can tell you that most moms are not seeing what they think they are seeing with these instruments. In fact, I suspect many well meaning moms are not even visualizing the tympanic membrane but rather seeing redness of the canal or other totally unreliable surrogates for diagnosing an ear infection.

To actually diagnose an ear infection, you need to see the tympanic membrane and the small bones that lie behind it,-- if those bones are obscured then you habe to consider the fact that there might be fluid behind the ear, but fluid does not mean infection. Seeing the tympanic membrane is not as straight forward or easy as you may think, and even in healthy ears with this otoscope seeing the little bones behind it is tricky. It takes most med students at least a month of looking in a dozen kids' ears per day to reliably find the tympanic membrane-- as a mom you are probably not finding it at all if you're just using it on your kids once every few months. You also have to be able to tell if the membrane is bulging or retracted and identify tiny perforations. These cheap scopes simply do not allow you to visualize such details.

It is nice as a mom to be able to tell yourself that you are being proactive, but do not kid yourself. If you have a high suspicion that your kid has a severe ear infection that hasn't gone away in 3 days (50% of them do), take him or her to the doc. Don't mess around with these things if you do not have the proper training or tools.

So if you like working on your printers more than printing this is the one for you. One week is all I've had this printer and I've had/have multiple problems. First off, right off the bat I noticed the bed has a huge bow in the middle. So if you level the build plate on all 4 corners, the nozzle slams into the build plate and jams. Just to get it to move without hitting I had to lower all corners 2-4times lower than they should be. So all prints fall apart unless they are directly on the bow, witch give me ruffly a 1.5in squared build area. Any bigger and the print will fail. Second, 3-4hrs of print time total on the machine (all of witch was spread out do to trying to get this thing to work) and the extruder fan locks up. So I had to order a new fan 3 days after receiving the printer. Now the most recent problem, the bed heater stopped working. The temperature jumps between 300-500c (max temp is 60c). Since it thinks the bed is already melting hot the heater will not turn on. I was well aware of this issue from other reviews but never in a million years did I expect it to happen within the first week and under 5hrs of print time. This plus the bow in the bed makes it impossible for any size print to stick. Yes it's a cheap 3d printer, but $200 or $2000 it should be expected to last longer than the first few hours of its first time being powered on. $200 price tag but this d@!$ thing should come with an Amazon gift card for all the parts you have to buy just to get it printing. I would not recommend this for anyone wanting to get into 3d printing that doesn't want to deal with a new headache every time you want to print. Expect to get the tools and your wallet out every time you turn it on. Right now I have a $200 paper weight until I decide if it's worth Dumping more time an money in.

I like to think that KVP manufacturers quality plastics.  Unfortunately, that quality means little when the product is ineptly packaged.  I ordered a 5-pound roll of KVP black ABS.  It was delivered bagged with a desiccant pack in a cardboard box.  But the top of the bag was not sealed correctly at the manufacturer, resulting in folds and wrinkles across the seam that prevented the bag from being air tight.  Further, the bag material is very thin and the plastic reel - shifting around inside the box - had worn holes through the bag in about a dozen places.  As a result, this product absorbed a lot of humidity between manufacture and delivery.  I dried the filament as best I could and it printed, but with visible steam coming out of the nozzle.  Not good.  Afterwards, the printed part did not match other components printed in KVP Black ABS.  That's because it is KVP Galaxy or Steller Black as opposed to "KVP Black" as indicated on the box and reel labels.  What a waste of time all around.  This will be going back to Amazon.  If KVP would invest in proper heat-sealing equipment and an extra dime per reel for more substantial  bags, they could save a lot of returns and customer disappointment.  Other filament - even low cost/low quality manufacturers - manage to hermetically seal their filaments through delivery.  I don't think it's rocket science.  If a manufacturer is selling a premium product, they should package it such that it's not ruined in distribution and delivery.

Photos: 3M tape is on the left, this tape is on the right.

Where to begin… I've worked in theater for over 4 years, and I've been in stage production for over 8 years total, so I know what gaffers tape should feel like. In total, I've probably used over 20 or 30 rolls of gaffers tape. From the moment that I unwrapped this roll of gaffers tape from the shrink wrap, I knew that I had made a mistake buying this.

The surface of the gaffers tape felt very flat, almost like it was made out of paper. When I tried to tear it, it was very difficult to do so. The underside of the tape had a super thin layer of adhesive, and also had no texture to it. The whole thing seem like coated tape to me, not like coated fabric like duct tape or gaffers tape should be. To verify my suspicions, I used my calipers to measure the thickness of the tape compared to some 3M gaffers tape that I had on hand still. This tape measured 0.18mm in thickness, while the 3M gaffers tape measured 0.28mm in thickness.

Looking at the photos that I included, you can see how this gaffers tape looks flat, untextured, and from the looks of it when you tear it almost like paper. In the last photo, you can see the layers of the gaffers tape separating, which just shows how poor quality this tape is. Sure, the 3M gaffers tape is 3 time more expensive. But even the $3 more [[ASIN:B00GZE3UJ8 Gaffer Power’s gaffers tape]] (which is what I'll buy when I'm on a budget) is miles ahead of this terrible excuse for gaffers tape. The only reason I jumped on this tape was because of Prime Day, but I learned my lesson. Spend 3 extra dollars and buy yourself some tape that you won’t regret.

Feb. 22, 2014
This item and the PowerSmith PAVC101 vac and PAAC301 filter have been grossly and dangerously misrepresented. from the start!!
The company video asserts the danger of how warm ash can burn thru a conventional vac but not with there's?
Warm ash contains small glowing embers that are not always evident in daily use.

Here lies the danger!
You can vacuum warm ash and when the added air flow thru the hose (which I must add is fire proof) mixed with unburned carbon in the ash, the warm ash will quickly turn to white hot sparks and burn thru the filter, pass thru the motor and be ejected strait up in the air thru the exhaust port while your happily looking at the wonderful job your doing on your stove and not seeing what's going on behind you!.

Then consider the erroneous assumptions from some users such as---
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Filter caught Fire? Impossible! It cannot catch fire - I do not believe the Reviewer - I vacuum warm (Sometimes glowing Hot) ashes all the time with no problems ever!

Q: Can you vacuum up warm ashes/ potentially sparks and have them safely stored in the can?
A: Yes, it works great for that. I do it often with my pellet stove.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This can contribute to deadly outcomes and everyone should be aware of this.
THIS SYSTEM IS NOT FOR USE WITH ANY WARM ASHES potentially containing even microscopic invisible embers!

When my 11 months old vacuum and 3rd filter burned thru, it melted the plastic basket surrounding the motor intake, melted the foam filter surrounding the motor, (which is NOT HEAT or FIRE PROOFED and not replaceable) and ejected embers and hot sparks straight in the air in my living room.

After a lengthy phone conversation with the parent company - Richpower Industries, Inc
for a replacement plastic basket, I also suggested to there RD department they incorporate a metal spark arrester and use a better grade of plastic components such as DuPont(tm) Zytel® PLUS nylon or HTN92 Series PPA, good to 230 deg. Centigrade.

When there customer service told me the plastic basket was not covered under warranty and tried to charge me $14.95, I was about to pack it all up and send it back to Amazon (2 year warranty) they relented and sent a replacement basket free of charge.

Here is the bottom line on why I am keeping it.
It has a robust 10Amp ball bearing motor with a cast aluminum fire proof impeller.
The hose is fire proof with metal lining.
Metal canister with good casters (great on a carpeted floor).
Easy to clean with great pulling power.
I intend to upgrade it with a metallic spark arrester on the motor intake and replace the foam motor filter with nonflammable fiberglass.

The basic design is sound, but it appears quality took the hit from the drawing board to the production with there overseas "manufacturing partners" (China).

Should Amazon pull this for safety concerns?
Not yet, but the company Richpower Inc. should at least be called to task on there deceptive, contradictory advertising. (140 deg. ash filter verse fire resistant hose and canister) after asserting other Vacuum can "potently become a fire hazard"? (like the PowerSmith PAVC101 won't do the same thing???)

I’m refurbishing an older boat and that includes redoing a lot of the wiring. These switches provide an easy-to-use on/off rocker switch for everything from navigation lights to bilge pump to fishfinder.

These are made to install in a control panel or box, let’s say, that is up to 1/8-inch thick. Any more than that and the spring-clips on the sides won’t click in. One drawback in the USA: the mounting hole you need is 20mm diameter, not a common size in a drill-bit. Apart from buying one in metric size, you’ll need to finesse a hole about 25/32nds of an inch, about a millimeter wider than a ¾-inch bit. I did it by rotating the bit a little in the hole.

This PEI sheet fits on both my Ender 3 V2 and Ender 3 S1 perfectly. My machines already had a magnetic base applied so I can't speak to the effectiveness of the one in this kit. I recommend pulling up a YouTube video on applying the magnetic sheet to get the least amount of air bubbles trapped under it.

The tabs on the edge make it easy to lift the PEI sheet from the magnetic base. They also help with lining the PEI sheet up before starting a print.

The texture carries through to prints perfectly. You may want to run your nozzle a little lower than normal to force the plastic into the pits and valleys of the textured surface. I found that the Z offset that I use for my smooth PEI sheets was about 0.1mm too high.

I had no problems printing both PLA and PETG on this sheet. In general, PETG worked better for me, but that's what I primarily print so my machines are better tuned for it.

This sheet only has PEI on one side, that side being the textured one. The other side is exposed steel. You could put some painter's tape, Kapton tape, or hairspray on the steel side to get some adhesion, but I wouldn't recommend using it. If you're looking for PEI all around, there are some vendors here on Amazon selling dual-sided sheets where one side is textured PEI and the other is smooth PEI.

For the best adhesion, I recommend washing this sheet out of the box with some dish soap and warm water. Use the soft side of a sponge and gently work the soap into the textured PEI. I think sometimes these manufacturers put a light powder on the PEI, and it's best to wash that off before use. After washing, hit it with a few passes of isopropyl alcohol or Windex, then you're ready to go.

At the time of writing this review, the price of this PEI sheet was $16.99. That's a good price for what you're getting, and at the time seemed to be one of the cheapest options here on Amazon. It may be an introductory price to gain some market share or reviews, but that price is good nonetheless.

The UNI-T UT301A+ Infrared Thermometer is a compact unit that comes with the thermometer, required single 9V battery, carrying case, and a simple manual. Activating the unit is as simple as flipping the red grip section forward and inserting the 9V battery, then closing the grip. Pulling the trigger gives you a reading, although, like me, you'll likely want to switch from Celsius to Fahrenheit first.

Consistency is what matters most, even above pinpoint accuracy, which is difficult with a consumer infrared thermometer. Fortunately, the UNI-T has excellent consistency when reading temperatures from the same spot. I was able to get good readings from various air conditioning vents, behind TVs and game consoles, and other areas I wanted to check for hot or cold spots.

The thermometer's temperature range is -25.6 to 788 degrees Fahrenheit (-32 degrees to 420 degrees Celsius), with an average 250ms response time. There's also a high/low temperature reading and alarm, as well as lock measurements. The manual succinctly describes operating distance and effectiveness, as well as the emissivity (energy radiation) of various materials. In short, the UNI-T provides everything the non-professional would likely need in such a device. It's highly recommended.

First, make sure to remove the fuse for the AC unit, you don't want to get shocked.

Second, take a picture of the wiring to make sure to put back everything where it supposed to be.

Third, use a screwdriver with a plastic handle in order to short the current capacitor. Cross the C common with the Fan then do the same with the
Herm, that should do it. You don't want to die so do it a couple of times.

Fourth, use a niddle nose plier to remove the connectors, do not attempt to pull on the wire as they may break

Fifth, remove the old capacitor and set the new one instead.

Sixth, plug the wiring back, close the unit and re-plug the AC fuse.

Seventh, test your AC!

Fairly simple unless your unit is on the roof like mine where I have only 2 feet of clearance between the AC unit and a 25 feet drop. So if like me, use a harness to secure your fall in case gravity is calling you back!

Enjoy 5 to 8 years of cooling....!

I've been wanting a backpack vacuum for awhile and finally made the purchase after getting 2 cats, and I am very glad that I did.  This vacuum has powerful suction and lots of accessories that work very well, and having the backpack makes vacuuming around furniture and the gauntlet of cat toys easy.  The quality feels very durable to me, and I like that the telescoping wand is metal (not plastic) and very sturdy. I use the self-powered "turbo brush" floor tool to clean 1000 sq ft of hard floors (wood, pergo, and vinyl), 400 sq ft of berber carpeting, and two low-pile area rugs, and this vacuum does a fantastic job picking up everything including lots of cat hair and litter.  And the vacuum does pick up in both directions, I usually do push and pull over same area due to all the cat hair/litter, but I can see the vacuum picking up in both directions.  The width of the "turbo brush" floor tool is perfect for getting between and under furniture, and I no longer have to move any furniture when vacuuming - it's just small enough to fit everywhere and the "neck" that attaches to the wand turns 360 degrees so I can twist it sideways and get it under cabinets.  An unexpected bonus for me is that this vacuum does a GREAT job dusting my wood furniture when I use the small rectangular attachment (not the dusting brush tool) - it gets up all the cat hair (in addition to the dust) very quickly.  I also love that it has a stable base and a carry-handle on top so if I need to do a quick pick-up in one spot, I just carry it over rather that put on my back and it stays in place.  I was a little nervous about the weight, but I have not had any problems wearing it for the 45 mins I usually spend cleaning (I am a 5'4" woman and reasonably fit).  It does blow warm/hot air out the side, but I consider this a non-issue because it's no hotter than my previous upright vacuum and far easier and quicker to use.  To me, the only negative to this vacuum cleaner is that it makes vacuuming and dusting so easy that I have no excuse not to do them.

Works great. I was able to find the dimensions from a different product [[ASIN:B0771W9M6R [initeq] Threaded Heat Set Inserts for Plastics Combination (Imperial + Metric) Assortment A 200 Pack]]. I used .206 in. for the top hole and .185 in. for the bottom hole, with a distance of .250 in. I also extended the .185 in. hole to the length of my screw. For the screw, I used [[ASIN:B000CZ4HFM The Hillman Group 101040 6-32-Inch x 1-1/2-Inch Flat Head Phillips Machine Screw, 100-Pack]].

I performed a stress test on this after setting it in a test block. I tried tweaking the screw sideways to see if the nut would come loose, but the screw bent. I then attempted to hammer on the screw from the back side (bottom side) of the nut test whether the nut would pop out. The screw bent, but the nut didn't budge. As a final test, I used a wrench to tighten the screw as far as I could. I expected the threads of the nut, being brass, would strip out or the nut would start spinning in the plastic. But... the head of the screw broke. :P I removed the remnants of the screw, and while there was slight damage to the threads, the nut still worked with a new screw without problem.

I was a little surprised I was not able to get the nut to even budge in the block. I printed with PLA, 5 layer outlines. I think this certainly helped to retain the nut. To insert the nut, I used my Weller WESD51 set to the lowest heat setting, which is 350 F. I didn't force the nuts in, but allowed the weight of the soldering iron to work the nut into position.

The only way these nuts are coming out of the PLA block is with heat. I'm pleasantly impressed with these, and this should allow me to expand the types of projects I can create with my 3D printer.

While this might seem pricier compared to glue sticks or hairspray its well worth the cost. Glue sticks worked so so for me. Hairspray worked but then left residue on the bottom to clean up. Also with hairspray you had to be careful not to overspray. With Magigoo you apply right on the area you want. You don't need to prep the whole bed unless you need to for a huge print. While the bottle says to apply new material to the bed each print, but I could get a lot more per application. But to be 100%, I would follow their instructions. Once the bed cools down you just simply take the part off by hand. The applicator tip ripped off and they sent me two replacements free of charge. I've printed with PLA, ASA, ABS, PETG with success with Magigoo. While you might get away with a cold bed for PLA, I've always had better luck with a heated bed and adhesive. I plan on getting their PC version shortly to print with Polycarbonate.

Oh ya some additional stuff: glue sticks also left residue to clean up. hair spray smell yuck. The number of prints varied if same model printed over and over in same spot. But I've gotten 5-20 per an application reducing cost per print a lot. To prep for use I clean off bed with hot water and dry. I spread on Magigoo where I need it and the material dries quickly.

These spools claim a consistent diameter of 1.75 give or take 0.05. Most spools I buy claim the same however I have not once actually /seen/ this amount of variance when measuring the diameter. Most spools seem to measure lows and highs of 1.73 - 1.76. Within a one foot stretch of this filament I can see 1.70 to 1.8mm depending on where I measure. That is within the product's described tolerance so I cannot fault it for that. But I cannot wonder if it is the cause of the slight variance in printed layers that is visible when under direct light. Printed 210/72 Prusa MK3S with full Bear Upgrade, textured PEI sheet. Pictures are after some basic extrusion multiplier adjustment and LA calibration @ .2mm layer height.

Like any filament purchase there are far too many variables to judge quality off of the finished print. Not to mention differences in color and batch. I have had small difficulties with adhesion but again that could just be me. I have not yet tried the black roll that I ordered.

Be ready for bruised hands if doing many of these without the proper crimper, but still these are perfect. Does exactly what you want for 4 Gauge wires. I crimped them with Vise-Grips, and with some technique they crimped nicely!

Vise-Grip procedure:
Insert twisted 4GA wire, and get all the little wires into the connector all at once using a careful twisting motion, should be plenty of space. Crimp slowly until the middle split starts to fold in. Individually crimp each side more, until looking inside the connector the metal goes from a "D" shape to a "B" shape, splitting the cable mostly in half to either side of the "B".

IMPORTANT: If connector is not in a "B" shape but looks like "6" or "9" you have messed up. Straighten out connector and try again. Otherwise the connection may pull free! This is not a product defect, but a technique error, work on it!

Some small wires will come out of the middle of the "B" while crimping, and that's ok. The black or red cable jacket will cover any errant little wires from the cable. There should only be a few. If many come out you have messed up with a "6" or "9". Straighten out the connector and try again.

If all is well and you have a nice "B" shape, I'd use another bigger pair of Vise-Grips to close the "B" into more of a "=", meaning I'd crimp the connector sideways to close off the "B", with emphasis on crimping the cable base here more than the ring side. This creates friction that guarantees a solid crimp.

Afterwards be sure to pull on the newly crimped connector, not with full strength but enough to ensure that daily usage will not disrupt the connection!

Good luck, and happy crimping. This is what you want for 4GA connectors, they are the best on Amazon, also buy these for the big 3. You won't regret it.x

I've gone through probably a half-dozen different kinds of organizers looking for a good way to keep track of small circuitry components. This is hands down the best one I've used for surface-mount components.

Sewing organizers and tackle boxes are better for larger parts, like things larger than your fingernail, but this is great for smaller stuff. The smallest parts I use are 0603, but I don't have trouble with anything falling out. The drawers also stay shut very well.

There aren't many cons, but the labels aren't very easy to write on. I just use a label printer to print part names out in a small font. The drawers are small, but I think it's a good compromise with how many there are. They're about 15mm wide and seem to fit about a thousand 0805 resistors comfortably. They're just large enough for a 0.5mm-pitch QFP100 chip to lie flat in, although you should probably use the pricier anti-static version of this box for things that require ESD protection.

Anyways, it's also small enough to put in a bag and carry around, which is very nice considering how many parts you can fit in it.

My old multimeter was from a big box tool store. It was a constant frustration. The leads were too short and needed frequent repair where they connected to the probe tips. It was time for a replacement.

Wow, I was pleasantly surprised when I received this meter. First off, the leads are plenty long for my uses, nearly twice the length of those of my old meter. The lead ends have strain relief and silicone shielding. Both are good features for longevity. The meter itself is solid and has a good feel in hand. The display is easy to read and is backlit.

The available tests are organized a bit differently than I’m used to, but nothing major. Several test types are combined under one dial setting, the test desired can be changed within each dial position by pressing the SEL (select) button. The test type displays on the meter screen and in the app, if connected. This meter displays temperature from the included probe in Fahrenheit or Celsius. I’ve not had a multimeter that displayed temperatures before and am looking forward to using it for various projects.

Having the app, enables easy reading and recording of values and even the ability to read the meter from a distance. The only limitation to reading via the app is to be within Bluetooth range. The app shows values on an analog dial, which is handy to quickly see changes in readings.

As others have mentioned, the battery cover requires a very small Phillips screwdriver, size 00. I did not have any issues installing the included 9V battery.

The package includes the meter, a pair of test leads, a temperature probe with coiled wire, a case, 9V battery and instruction book. (See pic)

I’m very happy with this new multimeter. My old meter is going out the door and I hope this review has been helpful.

These copper connectors are SC35-10 and are very solidly built. The set gives you 10 of the most common used lugs. It does not come with a crimping tool, but it does give you the heat shrink tubes which is an added bonus. I have a couple of different size crimping tools so this was not a big deal for me, but someone who doesn't have one may want to know it doesn't have one.
This set is not exhaustive, but it is very good set to have when you need it from time to time. Various size lugs will fit most applications, but there might be times when you'll have to go to the hardware store to find that specific size that you need. This is the new and improved set that you get, where quality standards and thickness have been increased.
The copper is high temperature resistant, as well as anti corrosion proof. They are commercial grade and very durable. A must-have for any DIYer, the lugs are 100% pure copper, and when fastened correctly, your wire will not slip out.
Only one criticism, the thickness of the terminals do not increase as the size goes up. For the smaller size lugs the thickness is more than enough. For the medium size lugs the thickness is perfect, but for the larger size lugs 2mm more would have been better. Yet, they did increase the thickness with this latest revision. Great value and I highly recommend it.

Regarding both DACS and amps, the law of diminishing returns starts at around $350 for the pair. The purpose of this pair is to take a digital signal from a computer device and make it into an analog signal that is sufficiently loud. Solid state amps do the best job at that, as they do not color, distort, mute, and add noises (popping, hissing, etc.) like tube amps do. As such, a $350 portable JDS Labs O2 amp and Standalone ODAC pairing will achieve 95% of the audio quality of any $5,000 or even $50,000 setup, marketing spam notwithstanding. A great alternative pairing is the $199 Schiit Magni 2 and Modi 2, but they are not portable and you may have to upgrade to the costlier Uber models of both (another $120 or so) to achieve compatibility with your equipment. Empirical evidence is minimal in the audio industry, which has opened the doors for outlandish manufacturers' claims that rationalize the ridiculously inflated prices of their products. Third-party measurements of sensitivity, efficiency, and the like are some of the few characteristics that can be objectively measured. Proud to support the American Worker. I replaced my condenser fan motor and capacitor four years ago on my 17 year old Trane. The old cap was still in specs but for very little money for a USA made capacitor it was a no brainer. I've used Genteq's in the past with no problems but their made in Mexico. I do like that Amrad warranties them for their licensed contractors customers for 5 years, that says a lot about their parts and quality control. I know it doesn't apply to me as a DIY but I'm ok with that. Two years ago Morris Jenkins replaced my neighbors HVAC system for $13,000. The first day it hit 96 degrees this summer their AC wouldn't work. They had no AC for hours by the time the tech came out to figure out the problem under warranty. It was the dual run capacitor and even he said they used cheap capacitors. I'd be ticked to find out I spent that much to have a cheap capacitor used and only last two summer seasons. Leaving my family in the heat on the first hot day of the next summer, ridiculous.

For DIY out there take care in replacing these. It's easy but can be dangerous make sure to watch videos on how to. Get a multimeter and pull the disconnect or shut the power off anytime you go to replaced one of these. Always re check for power at the contactor terminals plus remember to discharge the old capacitor. Next I will order a 10mf Amrad cap to replace my blower motor cap inside the house. It about four years old too but still in spec. Again, cheap quality replacements when you don't want the old ones to dump out when it's a hundred degrees outside where I live in South Carolina.

I've been buying this brand exclusively for many years now for pro AV work. There are a lot of tapes out there claiming to be "gaffer" tape that are nothing more than duct/duck tape with a matt finish. Most of them leave adhesive behind and some aren't even cloth backed. This is the real deal- it blocks light, has a matt black (if black is ordered) finish, and the adhesive, while strong, releases cleanly. Yes- it's more expensive- because it is the real thing. I have yet to have a cable, stand, carpet, wall, backdrop, mic, camera, speaker, or anything else ruined by this tape. I can't say that for cheaper alternatives I've tried.

I feel compelled to address some of the bad reviews I've seen:
Gaffer tape is gaffer tape! It is not duct/duck tape, and while it can do a lot more- it is designed to -temporarily- affix and mark items for stage and screen, photography, videography, lighting, AV, etc. It is not permanent, it isn't an automotive or construction adhesive, it isn't electrical tape, etc. If you leave any tape for months or years, or out in the sun- it is going to leave adhesive and probably damage something, or it is just going to come undone. If you aren't using it for its purpose- it will disappoint. That's not the fault of Pro Tape, or any real gaffer tape manufacturer.

My husband HATES to sweep and mop & what woman doesn't need her husband's help with housework? When our anniversary came around, I was looking for something he would "use" and something that would also be useful for me. So I got the Neato XV-21. This vacuum saves him so much time (and my sanity) it's unbelievable! The main level in our home is approximately 3100 sq ft. We have hardwood, tile, area rugs,and carpet. "She" will methodically work "her" way around the house and as "her" battery runs low "she" will work "her" way slowly back to the base to re-charge. Once the re-charging is complete "she" takes off again remembering where "she" left off. If I only need "her" to clean the common areas of the home (about 2100 sq ft) it will usually complete that with 2 charges(the starting one & one re-charge) unless we forget and leave "obstacles" on the floor, causing Neato to have to navigate more. If I have "her" clean the entire 3100 sq ft it'll take at least 3 charges. The only situations we've run in to that I would warn about are bar stools and a 1970's circular breakfast table, my husband & I turned into a pub table. The bar stool bases are just wide enough that "she" can go between the legs at an angle but can't get out. I put the bar stools upside down on the breakfast bar - problem solved. The pub table has one center post that goes all the way to the floor and 4 flat legs coming out from that base for the stabilization. Those legs are about 1 inch high at the highest point but "she" gets stuck on them. I put the barrier around it - another problem solved. The only downsides are (1)the kids leaving obstacles on the floor and no one is home to help "her" get them unstuck from her brush and (2)If I'm not going to have the time or don't want to sweep in the near future, I sweep around the walls, corners, and under the couch moving it all toward the middle of the floor so "she" can get all the dirt/dust("she" doesn't get neat to the walls very well). Also, not a downside, I noticed that the filter gets dusty very quickly even if you clean the dust bin often. I put in my extra one(I ordered extras) and put the dusty one in the dishwasher(as suggested by another reviewer)and it comes out as good as new. Just let it dry completely before using it again. I promise this, "she" has helped solved my frustrating issue of him not helping with housework when I have a full-time job and we have 3 kids, 2 of which play sports.
